podcast.title: Founding by Ahmet Ertegun (1947)
podcast.body: Atlantic Records was founded in 1947 by Ahmet Ertegun, a legendary and controversial record executive. Ertegun was instrumental in the career of Led Zeppelin, signing them in the late 1960s and supporting them as they became one of the biggest bands in history. "It was precipitated by the death of Amit Erdogan, the legendary and controversial record man who founded Atlantic Records in 1947."

podcast.title: Hip-Pocket Records Releases (1966)
podcast.body: Atlantic Records partnered with Filco and Ford in 1966 to release singles on Hip-Pocket Records. These thin, bendable plastic Flexi Discs were sold for $0.69 at Ford dealerships and Woolworth stores, featuring artists like Chuck Berry and Sonny and Cher. `"They got Atlantic, Mercury, and Roulette records to release singles this way, selling them for $0.69 at four dealerships and through Woolworth stores."`

podcast.title: Aretha Franklin's Breakthrough (1967)
podcast.body: The R&B-rooted label Atlantic Records signed Aretha Franklin in 1967, a move that brought "respect to Arita's name" and transformed her into "America's premiere vocal dynamo," ending her period of no big hits at Columbia. "But a switch to R&B rooted label Atlantic records in 1967 brought respect to Arita's name, and made her America's premiere vocal dynamo."

podcast.title: Ahmet Ertegun's Urgency for "Ohio" (1970)
podcast.body: The president of CSNY's record company, named Almitard in the transcript (likely Ahmet Ertegun), demonstrated extraordinary urgency by flying the master tape of "Ohio" on a red-eye flight from Los Angeles to New York. His demand for immediate release led to the strategic decision to pull "Teach Your Children" from the charts, despite its potential to reach number one, to ensure "Ohio" was released without delay. "President of our record company, a wonderful man named Almitard, who was him Los Angeles that night when we finished recording and he took tape and flew to New York on the red eye. He said, I want this out now."

podcast.title: New Country Music Division (1972)
podcast.body: In 1972, Atlantic Records Vice President Jerry Wexler, a renowned R&B producer, sought to establish a new country music division for the label. He identified Willie Nelson as an ideal first country artist to sign after hearing him play "Bloody Mary Morning" at a Nashville party. "He liked it and thought that this was what the new country music division of Atlantic Records needed. Willie Nelson would be a pretty good first country artist to sign for the label."

podcast.body: In late 1993, Atlantic Records, a major label part of Warner, persuaded the band that founded Epitaph Records (Bad Religion) to release their next album through them, marking a shift for the historically indie group. "the band that founded their own label, Epitaph Records, in 1980, were themselves persuaded to release their next album on a major, Atlantic Records, who were part of Warner."

podcast.title: Censorship of "Only in America"
podcast.body: Atlantic Records decided not to release The Drifters' version of "Only in America" in 1963. They were concerned that the song's satirical intent—black people singing about the American dream—would be perceived as tasteless in the prevailing racial climate, opting instead to have a white group record new vocals over The Drifters' backing track. "But Atlantic worried that in the racial climbers of 1963 the satire would seem tasteless, so they took the drifters backing track and got Jay and the Americans, a white group, to record new vocals."

podcast.title: Creating a Vanity Subsidiary
podcast.body: In the 1970s, the major label Atlantic Records created a special subsidiary called Swan Song specifically for Led Zeppelin. This practice illustrates how major labels establish "vanity labels" or "boutique labels" for their important artists, offering perceived indie street cred or enhanced creative control. "When Led Zeppelin ruled the world in the 1970s, their label Atlantic created a special subsidiary for them called Swan Song."

podcast.title: Creative Pressure on Big Wreck
podcast.body: Atlantic Records attempted to influence Big Wreck's sound for their second album, *The Pleasure and the Greed*, by suggesting they should sound like Nickelback. This was a clear attempt to achieve a more commercially packaged product, which clashed with the band's artistic direction. "I'd be sending them down to Atlantic and it was like, oh, this is what they mean... They need to nickel back."

podcast.body: Atlantic Records was the label for The Drifters. After Benny King left the group, Atlantic continued to release material from their vault, including songs with King's lead vocals and older records. The label also navigated significant personnel changes within the group and concerns over song content. "After King left, Atlantic started releasing whatever material they had in their vault, both songs with King's Leeds and older records from the earlier lineup of drifters."

podcast.title: Expedited Release of "Ohio"
podcast.body: Ahmet Ertegun, the head of Atlantic Records, played a crucial role in the rapid release of Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young's song "Ohio." Within just 10 days of its recording, Ertegun ensured the record was on the streets, enclosed in a sleeve featuring the text of Article 1 of the First Amendment, demonstrating an urgent response to the Kent State shootings. "Almit Erdogan, the head of Atlantic Records, took that record and within 10 days that record was on the streets in a sleeve with the text of Article 1 of the First Amendment"

podcast.title: Falling Behind in Alternative Rock (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, Atlantic Records found itself lagging in the burgeoning alternative rock scene, particularly after Nirvana's breakthrough with other labels. To rectify this, they recruited executive Danny Goldberg and subsequently hired A&R specialist Tim Summer to specifically "beef up Atlantic's alternative roster." "Atlantic Records, a label that had fallen behind in the alternative rock sweepstakes."

podcast.title: Graham Parker's Conflict and Departure
podcast.body: Graham Parker signed with Atlantic Records, his fourth label in a decade, for his album "The Mona Lisa's Sister." However, when he presented his demos and offered to produce the LP himself, Atlantic insisted he work with outside producers and add studio sheen. Parker flatly refused, leading him to leave the label and sign with RCA instead. "He just signed two Atlantic records, already his fourth label in a decade."

Blown away by their performance, they flew back to New York and expressed strong interest to their president, initiating a bidding war involving Warner Canada, Elektra, and Warner Brothers. podcast.body: Atlantic Records, through its executive Jerry Wexler, showed keen interest in releasing Dale Hawkins' "Suzy Q." This interest was crucial as Chess Records had delayed the single's release for ten months, and Wexler's ultimatum spurred Chess to finally put the record out. podcast.title: Lack of Follow-up Support in US
podcast.body: After the initial success of "Try Honesty" from Billy Talent's debut album, Atlantic Records chose not to release a second single in the US. The band believed this was because the label prioritized promoting "bigger artists" nearing Christmas, marking the beginning of their ongoing "open battle with America." podcast.body: Billy Talent signed an 80/20 split deal with Atlantic for the world and America, with Warner Canada handling Canada. The band met co-founder Ahmet Ertegun in his office during the signing, noting Jimmy Page's bow from "The Song Remains the Same" on the wall as a powerful symbol of the label's history. podcast.body: Since the 1950s, Atlantic Records played a major role in popularizing Rhythm and Blues, a term coined by its executive Jerry Wexler. The label was known for successfully crossing R&B over to white audiences while preserving its raw, soulful essence, a strategy that would later revitalize Aretha Franklin's career. "Since the 50s, Atlantic had played a major role in popularizing Rhythm and Blues, a term by the way that was coined in the early 50s by Atlantic Records executive Jerry Wexler."

podcast.body: Atlantic Records, a smaller label, participated in payola as a method to equalize opportunities against the larger, more established record companies. podcast.title: Skepticism Towards Hootie & the Blowfish
podcast.body: Despite signing Hootie & the Blowfish, Atlantic Records initially showed considerable skepticism and disinterest towards their debut album, *Cracked Rear View*. It was signed for a "meager advance," and the label's head of A&R even wanted to shelve it, deeming it "irreleasable." The band was nearly dropped after the album failed to sell outside the South in its first two months, highlighting the internal struggle for acceptance within the label. "Expectations for cracked rear view were exceedingly modest. ... their debut was met with skepticism, even disinterest across the label."

podcast.title: Tom Bell's Choice of The Spinners
podcast.body: Upon joining Atlantic Records, Tom Bell deliberately chose to work with The Spinners, a group he was already familiar with, over more established artists like Aretha Franklin or Donny Hathaway, believing that the latter two were self-sufficient and did not require his production input. "He had the opportunity to work with Aretha Franklin or Donnie Hathaway when he joined Atlantic, but he figured that they did not need him. So he looked over the roster and he saw the spinners who he was already familiar with."
